Some years reward momentum;  
some years test the quality of it.  
FY26 did both.
For Arvind Limited, this was a year shaped by volatility in global 
trade, tariff-linked disruptions, cost pressures, shifting sourcing 
decisions and a more demanding customer environment. It was 
also a year in which the Company delivered one of its strongest 
performances, consolidated revenues crossed ₹9,300 crores, 
EBITDA crossed ₹1,000 crores for the first time, margins improved, 
PAT grew, net debt reduced and return ratios strengthened.
The Company responded to a difficult operating environment 
with discipline: protecting customer relationships, improving 
productivity, strengthening working capital, scaling volumes, 
investing in growth platforms and remaining focused on long-
term value creation. Textile revenue moved close to ₹7,000 crores. 
Garmenting crossed ₹2,000 crores in revenue and recorded its third 
consecutive quarter of 10 million-plus pieces. Advanced Materials 
achieved its guided growth trajectory, supported by a stronger 
second half. During the year, Arvind also took a decisive step towards globalising 
its Advanced Materials platform through the acquisition of Dalco-
GFT via Arvind Advanced Materials Limited, marking its entry into 
the world’s largest technical textiles market. This is the essence of 
Strength that Adapts. 
It is the strength of an integrated textile and apparel platform 
that can respond to changing customer needs. It is the strength 
of a garmenting engine that is becoming more relevant to 
global sourcing shifts. It is the strength of an Advanced Materials Strength 
that Adapts4

business that is moving into higher-value, specialised and global 
opportunities. It is the strength of a balance sheet managed with

In a world where supply chains are being redrawn, customers

FY26 was a year in which Arvind Limited demonstrated the depth 
and adaptability of its business model. The 95th Integrated Annual 
Report presents that journey through the lens of performance, 
strategy, resilience, governance and long-term value creation.
The report covers Arvind’s business activities and performance 
for the period April 01, 2025 to March 31, 2026. It provides 
stakeholders with a consolidated view of how the Company 
delivered growth in a volatile operating environment, strengthened 
its financial position, scaled key business platforms and continued 
to invest in capabilities that support future competitiveness.
The theme for this year’s report, Strength that Adapts, reflects 
the core of Arvind’s FY26 story. It captures the Company’s ability 
to respond to changing market conditions with discipline through 
volume growth, cost optimisation, working capital rigour, customer 
engagement, manufacturing depth, sustainability-led operations 
and the continued scaling of growth platforms such as Garmenting 
and Advanced Materials.About the  
Report8
Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026

This report explains how Arvind creates value through its six 
capitals: Financial, Manufactured, Intellectual, Natural, Human, 
and Social & Relationship Capital. It connects financial outcomes 
with the operating decisions, investments, capabilities, risks 
and stakeholder relationships that shape the Company’s long-
term performance. This approach is consistent with the structure 
followed in Arvind’s previous Integrated Annual Report, which

In preparing this report, Arvind has considered the principles of 
the Integrated Reporting framework, the GRI Standards, the nine

Dear Shareholders

=== page 14 ===
Yet, Arvind responded with clarity, discipline and resilience. 
The Company delivered its highest-ever consolidated revenue 
and EBITDA during the year. Consolidated revenue grew 12% to 
₹9,303 crores. EBITDA crossed ₹1,000 crores for the first time, 
reaching ₹1,061 crores, with margins improving to 11.4%. Profit 
after tax before exceptional items grew 21% to ₹444 crores. Net 
debt reduced by ₹112 crores, supported by improved free cash 
generation and working capital discipline. Return on capital 
employed also improved during the year.
These outcomes are important but give them meaning in the 
environment in which they were delivered. FY26 was not a year of 
easy headwinds. Margin expansion was impacted by tariff-related 
pressures, and growth was moderated despite healthy demand. 
The Company also absorbed the one-time impact arising from 
the implementation of the new Labour Code. Yet, we continued to 
grow, improve efficiency, protect customer relationships, invest in 
capability and strengthen the balance sheet. At Arvind, strength has evolved with every shift in markets, 
technologies, customer expectations and societal priorities. It 
is visible in the way we are becoming more customer-centric 
and design-led; in the way we are using automation, digital 
systems and AI-enabled tools to improve efficiency, precision 
and responsiveness; in the way we are expanding into Advanced 
Materials; and in the way sustainability is shaping how we 
report progress as well as how we operate and grow. This is the 
spirit behind the theme of this year’s Integrated Annual Report,  
Strength that Adapts. This is the essence of Arvind.  
FY26 was a year that tested this adaptive strength.
The Indian economy continued to demonstrate resilience and 
steady growth through FY26, supported by robust domestic 
demand, continued government focus on infrastructure and 
manufacturing, and a stable policy environment. At the same time, 
the year presented its own share of headwinds: input cost volatility, 
uneven consumption trends in certain segments, and global 
spillovers that tested business planning.
The global operating environment remained complex and 
uncertain. Trade disruptions, tariff-related pressures, geopolitical 
shifts, inflationary trends and changing sourcing patterns created 
a difficult backdrop for manufacturing-led companies. For Arvind, 
with its deep export relationships, integrated textile capabilities 
and growing Advanced Materials portfolio, these developments 
directly influenced customer decisions, costs, margins, supply 
chains and planning cycles.This reflects the enduring strength of Arvind’s 
business model: a diversified portfolio spanning 
multiple geographies, product categories, 
capabilities, and business cycles. This strategic 
breadth and balance enable the organisation to 
navigate evolving market dynamics with agility 
while remaining firmly focused on its long-term 
growth ambitions and strategic priorities.

Our Textile business continued to demonstrate the relevance 
of integration. Denim volumes grew strongly. Woven fabrics 
reached an all-time high annual volume. The Garmenting business 
continued its strong trajectory, crossing the 10 million pieces mark 
for three consecutive quarters and reaching 42 million pieces for 
the full year.
It signals the continued evolution of the Company from a fabric-led 
enterprise to an integrated textile and apparel solutions partner to 
global customers. Today, customers are looking for partners who 
can provide reliability, speed, design responsiveness, product 
development, compliance and sustainability. Arvind’s integrated 
platform allows us to respond to these expectations with credibility 
and depth.
The world’s sourcing architecture is changing. Customers are 
diversifying supply chains, reducing concentration risk and 
seeking partners who can manage complexity with consistency 
and confidence. India has an important opportunity in this shift. 
Arvind, with its manufacturing depth, long-standing customer 
relationships, quality systems and growing garmenting capability, 
is well placed to participate meaningfully in this opportunity.
However, opportunity must always be matched by execution. Our 
focus, therefore, remains on building a more agile, efficient and 
responsive textile and apparel platform. We are strengthening 
design and customer proximity, improving productivity, increasing 
vertical integration, modernising operations and investing in 
automation and digital systems. The future of this business will 
be shaped not only by scale, but by our ability to respond faster 
and better to end-market needs. Our Advanced Materials business 
represents another powerful expression of Arvind’s ability 
to evolve.
Advanced Materials extends Arvind’s capabilities and knowledge 
of fibres, fabrics, coatings, composites and process capability into 
high-performance applications. It allows us to serve sectors where 
material science, application expertise, reliability and customer-
specific solutions are critical. These are areas that are structurally 
different from conventional textiles but deeply connected to 
Arvind’s core strengths.
The demerger of this business into Arvind Advanced Materials 
Limited gives it sharper strategic focus and greater ability to pursue 
its own growth path. As part of our five-year strategic roadmap, 
growth through the capture of inorganic opportunities remains a 
key lever — one that will add new dimensions to our business and 
accelerate our growth journey. During the year, Arvind Advanced 
Materials also entered the U.S. market through the acquisition of 
Dalco-GFT , at an enterprise value of approximately $136 million. 
This marks an important step into the world’s largest technical 
textile market and strengthens our presence in specialised  
non-wovens.
This is a meaningful milestone. It signals the ambition to build 
businesses that are rooted in India, but increasingly relevant to the 
world. We will build global businesses selectively and thoughtfully, 
in areas where we have capability, customer trust and a clear path 
to long-term value creation.Sustainability continues to be one of the most important 
foundations of Arvind’s future. For us, sustainability is a way 
of thinking about competitiveness. It influences how we use

About Arvind
Built on legacy. Strengthened by change. 
Arvind Limited is one of India’s most 
established textile, apparel and Advanced 
Materials enterprises, with a legacy that 
goes back to 1931 and a business model that 
continues to evolve with changing markets, 
customers and technologies.
At Arvind, scale has never been an end in itself. 
The Company has built its leadership by staying 
close to customer needs, investing ahead of shifts 
in the industry, strengthening manufacturing 
capabilities, and embedding sustainability 
into the way it operates. This ability to evolve 
with purpose defines Arvind’s journey and gives 
meaning to this year’s theme,  
Strength that Adapts.

=== page 18 ===
In FY26, this strength was visible across the business. The Company 
delivered record consolidated revenue of ₹9,303 crores and EBITDA 
of ₹1,061 crores, while Textiles, Garmenting and Advanced Materials 
continued to scale despite a volatile global trade environment. 
An Integrated Enterprise
Arvind Limited is an integrated solutions provider across textiles, 
apparel, Advanced Materials, environmental solutions and adjacent 
businesses. Headquartered in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, the Company 
serves an expanding base of domestic and global customers 
through deep capabilities across design, product development, 
manufacturing, innovation and sustainability-led operations.
The Company’s textile and apparel platform spans denim, 
woven fabrics, knits and garmenting. Its Advanced Materials 
business serves specialised applications across Human 
Protection, Industrials and Composites. This diversified 
presence enables Arvind to participate across both 
traditional and emerging growth segments, while reducing 
dependence on any single product, geography or market cycle. 
In FY26, Arvind’s textile business reported 
revenue of    ₹6,897 crores, up 12%, while Advanced 
Materials delivered revenue of ₹1,839 crores 
and maintained a full-year EBITDA margin 
of 15.1%.

=== page 20 ===
Scaling with Adaptive Strength
Transformation at Arvind is a continuous process. The Company 
has consistently evolved its capabilities to remain relevant to 
customers, competitive in global markets and responsive to 
emerging opportunities.
In Textiles, Arvind continues to strengthen its position across 
denim, woven fabrics, knits and garmenting. In FY26, denim full-
year volume reached 60 million metres, up 15%. Woven fabric 
volume reached an all-time high of 136 million metres. Garmenting 
delivered 42 million pieces for the year, up 12%, and crossed ₹2,000 
crores in revenue. 
In Advanced Materials, Arvind is building a higher-value platform 
across Human Protection, Industrials and Composites. The 
business achieved its guided 18–20% growth trajectory in FY26, 
supported by a stronger second half, favourable product mix and 
operating leverage. 
During the year, Arvind also advanced its global growth agenda 
through Arvind Advanced Materials Limited. The acquisition of 
a 61% stake in U.S.-based Dalco-GFT marked Arvind’s entry into 
the world’s largest technical textiles market and strengthened its 
presence in specialised non-woven materials. 
Key differentiators
• Pioneer in denim in India 
• Established capabilities across Advanced Materials, wovens, 
knits, voiles and garmenting 
• Integrated textile and apparel platform serving 
global customers 
• Advanced Materials platform across specialised and higher-
value applications 
• Long-standing sustainability leadership across water, energy, 
fibre and chemical management 
• Continued focus on innovation, traceability, circularity and 
responsible manufacturingRooted in Eco Consciousness 
Arvind’s sustainability journey is central to its business 
strategy. The Company’s focus on responsible manufacturing is 
reflected across fibre, water, energy, chemicals, circularity and 
climate action.
During FY26, Arvind continued to advance sustainability-led 
innovation. In partnership with H&M Group and Deven Supercriticals, 
the Company commissioned India’s first supercritical CO₂ dyeing 
facility at Santej, an investment of ₹25 crores. The technology 
has the potential to save up to 76% water, 67% energy and 90% 
chemicals in the dyeing process. 
The Company also strengthened its circularity agenda through 
its collaboration with Circ, aimed at integrating next-generation 
recycled fibres across operations. In addition, Arvind’s near-term, 
long-term and net-zero targets were validated by the Science Based 
Targets initiative, aligning the Company’s climate ambition with a 
1.5°C pathway to net zero by 2050. 
In FY26, Arvind’s S&P ESG score improved to 74, with the 
Company ranked 6th globally and 2nd in India as per the FY26  
investor update. 
For Arvind, eco-consciousness strengthens customer trust, 
improves resource efficiency, supports regulatory readiness 
and reinforces the Company’s long-term value creation model.

FY26 was a year in which the global operating 
environment became more complex, less 
predictable and more demanding for textile, 
apparel and Advanced Materials companies. 
Global trade remained volatile, tariff-related disruptions affected 
sourcing economics and customer decisions, geopolitical 
developments continued to influence supply chains, and customers 
became more cautious, more cost-conscious and more selective 
in choosing manufacturing partners. At the same time, the long-
term opportunity for India remained intact, supported by supply 
chain diversification, evolving trade agreements, strong domestic 
consumption and growing customer interest in integrated, reliable 
and sustainable sourcing partners.Adapting to a redrawn global 
textile and materials landscapeExternal Operating 
Environment22
Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026
=== page 24 ===
New Opportunities in a Shifting Trade Environment
Global sourcing is being rebalanced. Customers are increasingly 
evaluating manufacturing partners through the lens of supply 
assurance, geopolitical risk, compliance standards, sustainability 
readiness and long-term reliability.
India is well placed in this transition. As brands look to diversify 
beyond traditional sourcing geographies, India’s textile and 
apparel sector has the potential to gain share across categories. The 
free trade agreement with the UK, which imports USD 20 billion in 
textiles, of which India holds a 5% share, has further reinforced the 
nation’s supply chain strength. The Indian government’s policies 
and initiatives such as PM MITRA Parks, the PLI Scheme, and RoSCTL 
are further encouraging investment and catalysing expansion in  
the sector. 
Sharp focus on promoting technical textiles such as agro-textiles, 
medical textiles and geo-textiles has opened up new high-margin, 
growth-oriented avenues for companies to explore and harness. At 
the same time, the subsidies, tax exemptions and support offered 
by many states through new policies are aiding the sector’s growth. 
The recent downtrend in raw material prices is further promoting 
investments in the sector, which continues to seize the next set of 
growth prospects.
Integrated Capability as a Competitive Advantage
The global customer expectation is changing from product 
supply to solution partnership. Customers increasingly 
want suppliers who can support the full journey from 
material innovation and fabric development to garmenting, 
compliance, traceability and responsible manufacturing. 
This shift strengthens the relevance of integrated players. Sustainability as a Market Requirement
Sustainability is now central to competitiveness in textiles and 
apparel. Customers, regulators, investors and consumers are 
placing greater emphasis on water stewardship, energy transition, 
circularity, responsible fibre sourcing, chemical management, 
traceability and science-aligned climate action. These are no longer 
only ESG indicators; they are increasingly part of sourcing decisions 
and market access.
Arvind’s long-standing investments in sustainability give it strategic 
relevance in this changing environment. The Company’s work 
across renewable energy, water reduction, sustainable fibres, 
circularity, green chemistry and responsible manufacturing 
supports both risk mitigation and customer differentiation. 
Investing in the Next Set of Growth Levers
The next phase of industry growth will be shaped by companies 
that can adapt across five key levers:
• Technology and digitisation
• Integrated textile and apparel capability 
• Advanced and specialised materials 
• Capital discipline and operational efficiency 
• Sustainability, circularity and traceability 
Arvind’s strategy is aligned with these shifts. The Company 
continues to strengthen its core textile platform, scale garmenting, 
build Advanced Materials as a focused growth engine, invest in 
sustainability-led innovation and maintain disciplined financial 
management.
This is the operating context for Strength that Adapts, a world of 
volatility, but also one of significant opportunity for companies 
with the capabilities, discipline and resilience to respond.

=== page 25 ===
Our Approach  
to Materiality
Arvind adopted a double materiality approach in FY25, recognising 
the link between organisational success and environmental and 
societal well-being. This assessment is not treated as a one-time 
exercise. Through ongoing stakeholder engagement, the Company 
re-evaluates and validates material issues each year, incorporating 
emerging concerns into the materiality matrix. The outcomes 
are shared with the ESG Committee of the Board for review  
and sign-off. Focusing on what matters most
At Arvind, materiality is central to how we 
identify the issues that matter most to our 
stakeholders, our business resilience and our 
long-term sustainability agenda.
As the textile, apparel and Advanced Materials landscape 
evolves, the issues that influence value creation are becoming 
more interconnected. Resource availability, fibre sourcing, 
water stewardship, chemical management, energy transition, 
people practices, capital allocation, traceability, regulation and 
supply chain resilience are no longer separate considerations. 
They directly influence operating continuity, customer 
confidence, market access, cost competitiveness and long-term 
enterprise value.

Focus on Proactive Risk Mitigation
A disciplined framework for a  
changing environment 
Arvind’s risk management approach is anchored in a 
proactive and structured framework. The Company 
identifies, assesses, maps and manages risks on 
an ongoing basis, with the objective of protecting 
business continuity, stakeholder interests and long-
term growth.
The Company’s Enterprise Risk Management 
framework supports proactive identification and 
mitigation of existing and emerging risks. Materiality 
insights are increasingly integrated into this 
framework, including climate-related risks, which are 
becoming central to business resilience and global risk 
management. Arvind’s treatment of climate-linked 
risks is aligned with the recommendations of the Task 
Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures, and 
is guided by the principles of interconnectedness, 
temporal orientation, proportionality and consistency. 
This approach enables the Company to assess risk not 
only by category, but also by time horizon, potential 
business impact and strategic response.
Climate-related Risks at Arvind
Understanding physical and transition risks
Climate change has direct implications for textile and apparel 
value chains. It can affect raw material availability, agricultural 
productivity, water security, manufacturing continuity, energy cost, 
regulatory requirements and customer expectations.
Arvind evaluates climate-related risks through two broad lenses: 
 Physical Risks
These arise from climate-related events such as floods, droughts, 
heatwaves and other extreme weather conditions that can damage 
assets, disrupt operations, affect resource availability and increase 
operating costs.
Transition Risks
These arise from the shift to a low-carbon economy, including policy 
changes, emission reporting requirements, carbon-related costs, 
technology shifts, changing customer preferences and increased 
expectations on sustainable raw materials.
For Arvind, these risks are especially relevant because the business 
is connected to cotton-growing ecosystems, water-intensive 
manufacturing processes, export markets, customer due diligence 
requirements and evolving sustainability standards.

Value Creation 
Strategy
At Arvind, value creation is anchored in this belief. The Company’s 
strategy is built around disciplined investments across its six 
capitals: Financial, Manufactured, Intellectual, Natural, Human, 
and Social & Relationship Capital. These capitals are not viewed in

FY26 reaffirmed the strength of this approach. In a year shaped by

Robust Supply Chain Framework
Arvind Limited assesses its significant suppliers through a 
structured Supplier Sustainability Assessment that evaluates 
ESG performance across environmental, social and governance 
dimensions. This includes both desk-based reviews and on-site 
engagement, covering energy use, emissions, labour practices, 
and ethical governance. We collect certification details from our 
suppliers to assess their current level of compliance with recognised 
ESG standards and to gauge alignment with our sustainability 
expectations and Supplier Code of Conduct.
Suppliers are expected to adhere to leading frameworks, such 
as ISO 14001, GOTS, SA8000, SEDEX, and ZDHC. When suppliers 
undergo third-party certification audits under these standards, 
any compliance issues identified are raised as non-conformities 
(NCs). Suppliers are required to address and close these NCs 
within specified timelines to maintain their certification status. 
This process ensures transparency, risk mitigation, and continuous 
improvement across our supply chain.
A structured component of this assessment programme is a social 
compliance review of key yarn and chemical suppliers, conducted 
in alignment with the SA8000 standard. Under SA8000, suppliers 
and subcontractors are defined as entities in the supply chain that 
directly provide the organisation with goods or services integral to, 
or used in, the production of its goods — making yarn and chemical 
suppliers a primary scope for due diligence. SA8000’s Management 
System element requires organisations to apply due diligence to 
supply chain relationships, strengthening vetting processes for 
both new and existing members, and supporting supply chain 
members in adequately addressing non-conformances.
In FY26, Arvind conducted SA8000-aligned assessments of 50+ 
yarn and chemical suppliers, using a combination of virtual and 
physical assessment modes. These assessments evaluated supplier 
practices against the nine normative elements of the SA8000 
standard:
For more details, refer to our Supplier Sustainability Program & 
Process at https://www.arvind.com/sustainability/governance and

Future Forward Factories:  
Advancing Near Net-zero Manufacturing
In FY26, Arvind advanced its decarbonisation journey through 
the Future Forward Factories initiative, developed in 
partnership with Fashion for Good.
The initiative includes an open-source, modular blueprint for 
sustainable Tier 2 textile manufacturing and the development 
of a physical demonstration facility in Gujarat. The blueprint, 
tailored to Indian manufacturing conditions, is designed to 
support wider industry adoption of sustainable manufacturing 
practices. The initiative is supported by partners including 
Laudes Foundation, Apparel Impact Institute and IDH, and is 
intended to demonstrate that sustainable manufacturing can 
be both scalable and commercially viable. 
For Arvind, this initiative reflects a clear strategic direction: 
manufacturing competitiveness must increasingly be built 
around resource efficiency, lower emissions, water stewardship, 
worker well-being and industry-level collaboration.

The Company’s approach is to reduce environmental impact while

Fibre lies at the heart of Arvind’s textile operations, with cotton as 
a principal raw material. Arvind has identified fibre, particularly 
cotton, as having high environmental and social significance 
through its double materiality assessment. The Company’s fibre 
strategy focuses on responsible sourcing, traceability, innovation

Arvind continues to promote sustainable materials, including Better 
Cotton, Organic Cotton and Regenerative Cotton. The Company 
also works to reduce dependence on virgin materials by increasing 
the use of recycled fibres and other sustainable materials such as 
Tencel and Hemp.
Traceability is an important part of this approach. Arvind uses 
platforms such as TrusTrace, Textile Genesis and Transparency-One 
to track cotton through the supply chain. The Company also follows 
recognised chain-of-custody standards, including GOTS, OCS and 
RCS, to strengthen assurance around responsible sourcing.
Avoided Emissions from Low Carbon Products - Cotton is our key 
raw material and majority of our products are made from Cotton. 
Cotton grown through organic cultivation practices (Organic 
Cotton) and Better Cotton Principles (BCI cotton) are the low 
carbon products in our product portfolio. We conducted an external 
Life Cycle Assessment to estimate the quantum of environmental 
impacts of conventional cotton in comparison with organic cotton 
and BCI cotton (Shah, Bansal, & Singh, 2018).
In FY 2025-26, 51% of our cotton was sourced from sustainable 
sources which led to an avoided emission of 21,796 MT Co2e. The 
total avoided emissions are calculated on the basis of emissions 
which would have occurred if 100% of the cotton sourced had 
been conventional. The emission factors from (Shah, Bansal, & 
Singh, 2018) were used for the estimation of avoided emissions. For 
estimating the percentage of revenue generated from low carbon 
products, we have used the share of sustainable cotton in our total 
cotton consumption. This share is then allocated to our revenue 
generated from textiles to get a revenue figure. Responsible Sourcing

Water stewardship reduces operating risk, supports 
manufacturing continuity and strengthens relationships with 
customers, suppliers and communities.Water Stewardship
Water is one of the most material resources for textile 
manufacturing. Arvind treats water conservation as a cornerstone 
of its sustainability efforts, supported by a zero-freshwater 
philosophy in manufacturing operations, recycling technologies 
and stakeholder partnerships. 
The Company regularly monitors water usage across facilities 
and uses this data to identify efficiency opportunities in high-
consumption processes such as dyeing, finishing and washing. Its 
water reduction approach includes low-liquor dyeing machines, 
optimisation of rinse and wash cycles, process recipe improvements 
and employee awareness programmes.W ater is essential to our operations and the 
communities we serve. W e adopt a holistic, circular 
approach to steward water responsibly across our 
value chain.
Arvind also operates Zero Liquid Discharge facilities across 
multiple locations, enabling reuse of treated effluent within plants.

Supplier Water Risk Assessment
We extend our water stewardship approach across the value chain 
through a comprehensive supplier water risk assessment. Using 
tools such as the WWF Water Risk Filter and the WRI Aqueduct Tool, 
we map our Tier 1 suppliers to their respective river basins and 
assess both basin-level risks—such as water scarcity, stakeholder 
conflict, and ecosystem health—and operational aspects like water 
use and discharge.
Since a majority of our suppliers operate in regions identified 
as high water-stress zones, we recognise the need for deeper 
engagement and shared action. To facilitate this, we established 
the Global Water Innovation Centre for Action (GWICA), which 
serves as a collaborative platform to work with suppliers and 
other stakeholders on advancing water stewardship and managing 
shared water risks. Based at our Santej facility in Ahmedabad, 
GWICA is a cross-sector platform to drive innovation, collaboration, 
and capacity building in water stewardship across the apparel 
industry.
On the knowledge front, GWICA expanded the scope of its 
work beyond water stewardship to encompass interconnected 
environmental challenges in collaboration with leading academic 
institutions. On capacity building, GWICA strengthened its pipeline 
of next-generation water stewardship practitioners by hosting 
immersive learning engagements for university students, providing 
direct exposure to industrial water management systems, treatment 
infrastructure, and applied research — bridging the gap between 
academic understanding and on-ground practice. On convening, 
GWICA brought together a diverse cross-section of stakeholders — 
including NGOs, industry practitioners, researchers, policymakers, 
and civil society organisations — to advance basin-scale approaches 
to water governance, with particular emphasis on community-led 
stewardship and the role of women in water decision-making.knowledge 
and advocacy, capacity 
building, andcross-sector 
collaboration.In FY26, GWICA deepened its impact across its three core pillars:Responding to Water Quantity Risks
To address risks related to the availability of water in stressed 
regions, GWICA supports the adoption of water-efficient 
processes and advanced recycling technologies among suppliers 
and manufacturers. The Centre offers water audits, technical 
consultations, and pilot implementation programmes to help 
facilities optimise consumption and become less dependent 
on freshwater.
Mitigating Water Quality Risks
Water pollution remains a pressing issue for the industry. GWICA’s 
state-of-the-art laboratory enables precise effluent analysis and 
supports the development and adoption of best-in-class treatment 
technologies. Through this, we aim to improve wastewater 
quality and ensure that discharges meet or exceed regulatory and 
environmental standards.
Navigating Regulatory Risks
As water policies evolve, staying ahead of regulatory changes 
is critical. GWICA provides advisory support to help suppliers 
and facilities comply with water use and discharge regulations. 
The centre also helps optimise treatment schemes and reduce 
operational costs—ensuring facilities are both compliant 
and efficient.
Collaborating with Stakeholders
Water is a shared resource, often involving competing users within 
a basin. Through GWICA, we create opportunities for dialogue and 
cooperation between brands, suppliers, NGOs, regulators, and 
community representatives. This collaborative approach helps us 
understand basin-wide pressures and mitigate the risk of conflict 
over shared water resources.
Climate Action and Energy Transition
Replacing coal with biomass
Our backward supply chain integration of biomass briquettes is 
ensuring continual supply of briquettes to replace coal as a clean 
and renewable energy source.  Besides reducing coal consumption 
to meet the Company’s energy needs, this helps protect the health 
of farmers by reducing the risk of pink bollworm and burning of 
cotton stalks.
In FY26, the Company utilised 24,565 MT from its biomass supply 
chain – an increase of 48% over the previous year. We are also 
advancing a torrefaction project as part of our biomass technology 
roadmap, which will further improve the energy density and 
efficiency of our biomass fuel, reducing dependence on coal across 
our boiler network.
Internal Price of Carbon
Given our largely domestic footprint, we introduced an internal 
carbon pricing mechanism in 2020 anchored to India’s evolving 
carbon pricing landscape — initially benchmarked to the Clean 
Energy Cess, a levy on coal aimed at discouraging fossil fuel use, 
which was later subsumed into the GST Compensation Cess. We 
initially set our internal shadow price at USD 2.5 per metric tonne 
of CO₂e. To stay aligned with both local policy direction and global 
benchmarks, we reference the OECD’s carbon pricing series as our 
64
Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026
=== page 66 ===
primary external calibration source. The OECD’s Pricing Greenhouse 
Gas Emissions 2024 report — based on 2023 estimates — confirms 
that India’s Net Effective Carbon Rate (Net ECR) is EUR 7.23 per 
tonne of CO₂e, driven entirely by fuel excise taxes (EUR 7.40 on 
average), as India does not yet levy an explicit carbon tax or operate 
an emissions trading system. This figure is broadly unchanged from 
our prior reference point. On this basis, we maintain our internal 
price at USD 5.25 per tonne of CO₂e, which reflects local relevance 
while remaining calibrated to an internationally recognised 
benchmark.
However, the carbon policy context in India is shifting materially. 
In June 2023, the Government of India officially introduced the 
Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), a rate-based Emissions 
Trading System, and adopted detailed compliance regulations in 
July 2024. In 2026, nine sectors — including textiles — will transition 
from the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme into the CCTS 
Compliance Mechanism. The OECD’s Effective Carbon Rates 2025 
report, published in November 2025, confirms that India is currently 
developing its ETS, and notes that the geographical coverage of 
carbon pricing is set to expand as India finalises its scheme. As 
CCTS compliance obligations become real for the textiles sector 
from FY 2026–27, Arvind’s internal carbon price will serve as an 
important preparatory instrument, both for investment appraisal 
and for building the institutional readiness needed to engage with 
an emerging compliance market.
The internal carbon price is factored into a range of business 
decisions, including capital expenditure, operations, innovation, 
sourcing, and supplier engagement. Although primarily applied 
qualitatively, it has begun influencing real outcomes. For example, 
our shift to biomass-based boilers — replacing coal-fired systems. 
In some cases, the price is integrated into cost models to lower 
return-on-investment thresholds for energy-efficient or low-carbon 
projects. This approach supports a range of strategic goals:
By assigning a value to carbon, we are embedding climate 
consciousness into the core of our operations. As the Indian 
Carbon Market matures and CCTS obligations become binding 
for the textiles sector, our internal pricing discipline positions us 
to navigate compliance proactively rather than reactively, and to 
continue strengthening this approach as it becomes more deeply 
integrated into our business processes.Encouraging internal 
behavioural change

Avoided Emissions
Avoided Emissions for Third Parties - We are manufacturer of textiles, 
and our emissions are mostly covered in the Scope 3 emissions 
of our customers. Any initiatives that we take to reduce our GHG 
emissions help our customers to avoid emissions. An example of 
such initiative is increasing the sourcing of renewable electricity in 
our electricity mix. Electricity is used in various textile processes, 
the integration of renewable energy helps us avoid emissions that 
would have occurred if we sourced 100% of our electricity from 
the grid.
In the FY 2025-26, 37% of our sourced electricity was renewable. 
This has led us to avoid an emission of 1,00,890 MT Co2e. The 
CEA emission factor for electricity was used for estimating the 
avoided emission.

Chemical Management
Chemical management is essential to responsible manufacturing. 
Arvind’s approach focuses on safer inputs, compliance, reduced 
consumption, improved discharge management and process 
innovation.
The Company’s chemical compliance is supported by systems 
and tools such as FTIR spectrometers and HPLC systems, which 
help strengthen adherence to MRSL and RSL requirements. This 
supports both operational vigilance and risk mitigation in relation 
to restricted substances in the value chain.
Chemical reduction is also supported by process innovation. In 
FY26, Arvind commissioned India’s first supercritical CO₂ dyeing 
facility at Santej in partnership with H&M Group and Deven 
Supercriticals. The technology has the potential to reduce water 
consumption by up to 76%, energy requirements by 67% and dyes 
and chemicals by 90% in the dyeing process. At Arvind, we combine natural wisdom 
with advanced innovation to transform our 
operations and create long-term value for 
people and planet.
Responsible chemical management strengthens compliance, 
reduces environmental impact and supports customer 
requirements for safer and lower-impact production
In FY26, on an average, 98.3% of the chemicals used in our 
manufacturing facilities were compliant with ZDHC MRSL.WHY IT

Risk Assessment Approach
Our risk assessment framework is central to our Chemical 
Management System. It includes:
Comprehensive Documentation: For every chemical used, we 
require submission of Technical Data Sheets (TDS), Material Safety 
Data Sheets (MSDS), Chemical Inventory Lists (CIL), Product Safety 
and Information Documents, and certifications for ZDHC, REACH, 
OEKO-TEX, and GOTS (where applicable). Test reports from NABL-
accredited or third-party labs are also mandatory.
Analytical Testing Infrastructure: We operate advanced internal labs 
equipped with HPLC (High-Performance Liquid Chromatography) 
and FTIR (Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy), supported by 
a proprietary database of chemical substances. These tools help 
us screen incoming chemicals and proactively eliminate restricted 
substances from our operations.
Traceability via ZDHC Gateway: Our entire chemical inventory is 
uploaded to the ZDHC Gateway, where it is screened against the 
ZDHC Manufacturing Restricted Substances List (MRSL). This list 
is widely recognised and aligns with, and often exceeds, global 
regulations such as:
• EU REACH (Annex XVII, Candidate List)
• EU & UK POPs Regulations
• India’s List of Hazardous and Toxic Chemicals
• US EPA List of Lists, among others.Embedding Risk Management in Decision-Making
Our chemical risk management approach is not a standalone 
process—it is fully embedded in daily business decisions. It informs:
• Procurement and sourcing policies
• Product development and design
• Operational processes and SOPs
This integrated risk lens is supported by a robust monitoring and 
compliance.
Monitoring and Compliance
As part of our Chemical Management System (CMS) and in line 
with our Chemical Management Policy, no chemical is allowed into 
production without prior approval. This ensures that 100% of our 
product portfolio is monitored for the presence and use of non-
compliant substances. As of FY26:
 •  All facilities are progressing toward full ZDHC MRSL 
conformance. Substitution of remaining non-conforming 
C6 chemistry continues as part of our ongoing chemical 
management programme.
This reflects the success of our substitution strategies and our 
commitment to minimising hazardous substances in our products.
By combining rigorous documentation, analytics, regulatory 
alignment, and traceability, we ensure that chemical safety is not 
only a compliance measure—but a cornerstone of responsible 
manufacturing at Arvind.

Biodiversity and Ecosystem Resilience
Arvind recognises that textile and apparel value chains can 
affect biodiversity through soil degradation, changes in natural 
ecosystems and waterway contamination. The Company’s 
biodiversity approach includes identifying business-biodiversity 
relationships, assessing dependencies and impacts, and monitoring 
biodiversity-related risks and opportunities in line with the SBTN 
AR3T framework. 
The Company’s mitigation approach includes regenerative 
agriculture practices, transition towards deforestation-free supply 
chains and incorporation of biodiversity metrics into operational 
standards through certification alignment. 
For FY26, biodiversity is also linked to broader climate and resource 
risks. FY26 materiality input notes that biodiversity loss, extreme 
weather events and natural resource constraints have implications 
for cotton-growing geographies, water availability and the long-
term viability of natural fibre  supply chains.Natural capital is visible in how Arvind sources fibres responsibly, 
conserves water, improves energy mix, manages chemicals, 
advances circularity and invests in lower-impact technologies. It 
is also visible in the way the Company treats sustainability not as 
a standalone agenda, but as a core driver of customer relevance, 
resource resilience and long-term value creation.

The resulting action plan for conserving biodiversity across 
operational areas includes: 
 •  Adoption of regenerative agriculture practices to restore the 
productivity of agricultural land, 
 •  limiting agricultural expansion to existing areas; 
 •  Transition to deforestation-free supply chains — with a 
commitment to no gross deforestation by 2030 for critical 
commodities including cotton and viscose — through 
sourcing from existing managed landscapes for agriculture 
or forestry activities; and
 •  Incorporating biodiversity metrics into operational 
standards through alignment with certification standards. 
Compliance is tracked through a resilient compliance framework 
encompassing sustained supplier and partner engagement for 
effective management and mitigation of deforestation risks, 
concerted measures to ensure Group-wide compliance with 
forest regulations and mandatory standards, and performance 
measurement based on metrics identified as part of Arvind’s 
biodiversity strategy. 
Beyond avoidance, Arvind’s biodiversity commitment also includes 
adopting the mitigation hierarchy of avoid, minimise, restore and 
offset when operating near critical biodiversity areas, defining 
biodiversity-related targets to reach no net loss, and conducting 
regular biodiversity risk assessments across its own operations and 
value chain.For FY26, biodiversity is also linked to broader climate and resource 
risks. The WEF Global Risks Report 2026, which Arvind references 
in its FY26 materiality assessment, confirms that biodiversity loss 
and ecosystem collapse is the second highest long-term global risk 
over a ten-year horizon. This is directly material for Arvind given 
that cotton-growing geographies — spanning over 1,45,000+ Ha 
across Better Cotton, organic and regenerative programmes — are 
exposed to extreme weather patterns, soil health pressures and 
freshwater scarcity, all of which affect the long-term viability of 
natural fibre supply chains and the communities that sustain them.
Natural capital is visible in how Arvind sources fibres responsibly, 
conserves water, improves its energy mix, manages chemicals, 
advances circularity and invests in lower-impact technologies. It 
is also visible in the way the Company treats sustainability not as 
a standalone agenda but as a core driver of customer relevance, 
resource resilience and long-term value creation.

Farmer Ecosystems and Sustainable Cotton
Cotton is central to Arvind’s textile operations, making farmer 
relationships strategically important.
Arvind’s sustainable cotton work connects business continuity 
with farmer capacity-building, responsible sourcing and  
environmental stewardship. 
In FY26, Arvind reported engagement with 85,000+ farmers, support 
across 1,45,000+ hectares of sustainable cotton cultivation, and a 
10% premium paid to farmers for organic and regenerative cotton 
over market price. 
Sustainable Cultivation Practices
We actively promote adoption of practices that improve soil health 
and aid the restoration of organic carbon in the soil. 
• Implementing Regenerative Organic Certified (ROC) and 
Regenagri programme that focus on rebuilding soil health, 
enhancing biodiversity and improving farmer resilience.
• These practices include crop rotation, composting, minimal 
tillage, and eliminating synthetic inputs, all aimed at restoring 
the natural ecosystem.
• Through regenerative agriculture, we aim to sequester carbon, 
improve water retention, and create long-term value for 
farming communities. 
• Use of non-GM seeds, as well as zero chemical pesticides 
and fertilisers, to farm organic cotton, driving a positive 
environmental impact.
• Making the land organic through in-conversion organic, giving 
the land time to rid itself of previously used substances; we aim 
to extend this support to more farmers.
• Aimed at improving cotton quality through efficient water use 
and application of approved fertilisers and pesticides. 
• 68,000+ farmers reached through this initiative in FY26. Regenerative Agriculture
Organic and in-conversion organic 
Better CottonFarmer Engagement and Social Responsibility
True sustainability goes beyond environmental stewardship, thus in 
our Fibre programmes we also focus on fostering ethical, safe and 
inclusive practices in the communities that grow our fibres. This is 
done by:
• Raising awareness of labour rights through capacity building 
sessions with farmers covering topics such as fair wages, safe 
working condition, no child labour, no forced labour, etc.
• Promoting gender equality and non-discrimination 
by encouraging the participation of women and  
marginalised groups.
• Monitoring field-level implementation through regular 
assessments.
• Supporting farmers’ welfare through fair pricing and premium 
payments for organic produce.
Circular and Alternate Fibres
To drive circularity and reduce reliance on virgin inputs, we are:
• Scaling up use of recycled fibres (post-consumer and post-
industrial)
• Operating in-house mechanical recycling and collaborating 
with innovative companies like PurFi to recycle post-industrial 
and post-consumer textile waste while maintaining fibre 
quality. Under the Fashion for Good umbrella, we are advancing 
work on the Future Forward Factories (FFF) initiative, the 
Advanced Processing Matrix, and the Fibre Circularity Transition 
Programme (FCTP). 
• Investing in R&D and product development to focus on 
alternative fibres like Bamboo, Flax, Hemp, Banana, Altag, 
etc. We expanded this programme further with trials on 
Indian Nettle Urtica dioica bast fibre and other natural fibres, 
alongside the initiation of textile-to-textile polyester recycling 
trials to advance circularity in synthetic fibre streams.

Creating Lasting Value for People and Planet
Founded in 1931 at the height of the Swadeshi movement, Arvind 
was built on a conviction that Indian enterprise could match 
the world; and in doing so, contribute to a nation finding its 
independence. Industry and nation building were, from the very 
beginning, the same endeavour.
That same pioneering instinct has always extended beyond the 
factory floor. As Arvind grew into a global textile leader, it carried 
with it a belief rooted in the Lalbhai legacy, that a healthy business 
can only operate in a healthy society. Being firm believers that wealth 
created through enterprise carries an obligation to strengthen the 
communities around it. This is the foundation of what Arvind calls 
being a good neighbour.First Movers in Industry.  
Long-Term Partners in Community.
Being a good neighbour means listening closely, partnering 
deeply, and investing in what communities need most, whether 
in education, livelihoods, or environmental resilience.  Over time, 
this commitment has matured from philanthropic intent into 
structured, outcome-driven development, implemented through 
Arvind Foundation and a network of trusted partners.
This year, we take that evolution a step further. Our CSR work is 
presented through a goal-driven framework, where each goal 
reflects a long-term development priority, and each programme is a 
lever in service of that goal. It is the same approach that has guided 
Arvind in industry for nearly a century: begin with the end in mind 
and build purposefully toward it.

Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026
=== page 88 ===
In India, the distance between completing school and securing a 
sustainable livelihood remains one of the most consequential gaps 
in human development. Arvind’s work in this space is focused on 
closing that gap equipping young people with the skills, confidence, 
and opportunities they need to move from education into 
meaningful employment and economic independence.
Where It Begins: The GYANDA Programme
SDG 4 calls for inclusive, quality education. SDG 8 calls for decent 
work and economic growth. For millions of children in India, the 
distance between these two goals is where opportunity is lost, 
enrolment has grown, but learning outcomes, employability, and 
economic mobility have not kept pace. The link between education 
and livelihood, which these goals assume, must be actively built.
Launched nearly two decades ago by SHARDA Trust, GYANDA 
is designed to bridge that gap. In a classroom, a child from an 
underserved household is rarely more than a roll number. Without 
individual attention or broader exposure, school completion 
becomes the ceiling rather than the foundation and the trajectory of 
the parent becomes the trajectory of the child. GYANDA is designed 
to break that pattern.
Working with students from Grades 5 to 12 from government 
schools, the programme builds academic foundations, digital 
fluency, and 21st century skills through structured after-school 
learning aligned with the local board curriculum. It widens 
horizons, builds aspiration, and develops the skills that open doors Enabling Seamless  
School-to-Work Transitions
to opportunities the previous generation could not access. The 
measure of its success is generational. Success means this will be 
the last generation in poverty.
 
In FY26, GYANDA reached 820 students across four centres. 
An alumni study conducted this year offers a longitudinal 
view of the programme’s impact across careers, households,  
and generations.
 Improving numeracy through First in Math
According to the ASER 2024 report, more than 50% of Class 8 
students in India cannot perform basic division, a numeracy deficit 
that quietly forecloses career options long before a student reaches 
the workforce. This year, Arvind partnered with First in Math, a 
globally recognised digital mathematics platform, to strengthen 
numerical reasoning among GYANDA students.
Across three centres, 463 students collectively solved 4,87,011 
problems. One of our centres even achieved a ranking among the 
Top 100 schools nationally on the platform, proving what focused, 
technology-enabled learning can accomplish.

Beyond school: The Scholarship Programme
The GYANDA alumni study found that 61%  of respondents believed 
that without structured support, they would have faced an absence 
of both education and income.  This is not unique to any single 
programme, across India, the transition to higher education is 
where potential most frequently stalls, not for lack of ambition, but 
for lack of means.
Arvind’s scholarship programme exists to remove that barrier. 
Offered to need-based students across Ahmedabad and 
Gandhinagar. Administered in partnership with Vidyasarthi through 
a transparent and rigorous selection process, the programme 
covers tuition and essential academic costs, ensuring that financial 
circumstance does not determine educational destiny.
In FY26, the programme supported 340 students towards  
a pathway of independence and empowerment.88
Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026
=== page 90 ===
As a textile company, Arvind’s value chain begins in the field: cotton, 
the foundation of much of what we make, is grown by smallholder 
farmers whose resilience shapes the long-term sustainability of the 
entire industry. 
Yet the farmers we work with through our CSR programmes are not 
just our suppliers; they are our neighbours. The challenges they 
face, including depleted soils, water scarcity, and rising input costs, 
are ones no market mechanism alone will solve. Investing in their 
resilience is both an expression of our good neighbour philosophy 
and a recognition that a sustainable industry must be built on a 
sustainable agricultural foundation.  
Biochar: Regenerating Soil
For farmers, soil health is everything and across Gujarat, decades of 
intensive agriculture have left soils depleted, less water-retentive, 
and increasingly dependent on chemical inputs. Biochar, a carbon-
rich material produced by transforming locally sourced cotton 
biomass, offers a different path: enriching soil health, improving 
water retention, and reducing dependence on chemical inputs 
through an ancient practice validated by modern science.
Three years ago, Arvind began cautiously piloting the programme 
with just 100 farmers to test whether biochar could deliver 
meaningful results in local conditions. The early promise was 
clear. In FY26, that pilot has grown into a programme reaching 
697 farmers  across 530 acres , with 158 metric tonnes  of biochar 
produced from locally sourced biomass and distributed free of cost, 
alongside hands-on training and field demonstrations. 
The programme promises to be a model with significant potential 
for scaling across India and beyond, offering smallholder farmers 
across India a low-cost, climate-resilient path to soil regeneration.
Watershed Management: Rainfall to Root 
Water is among the most critical and most precarious inputs a 
farmer depends on. In Botad, water security hinges on a single 
season: when the monsoon arrives in short, intense bursts that run 
off before they can be absorbed, groundwater levels decline and the 
window for productive farming narrows.Strengthening Farmers to Uplift 
Rural Economies
Arvind addresses this through two distinct but complementary 
initiatives. The micro-irrigation revolving fund supports farmers in 
transitioning to drip irrigation ensuring every litre of available water 
reaches the crop efficiently. Check dam repair and construction work 
at the landscape level, enable groundwater recharge and extend 
water availability through dry seasons. Together, they address the 
same challenge from both ends: securing water and using it wisely 
where it is needed.

Plantation: Rooting Climate Action in Community
The biochar programme rebuilds carbon in the soil. The watershed 
initiative secures water across seasons. Plantation completes this 
cycle, restoring green cover, strengthening soil, and supporting the 
ecological balance that communities depend on.
At Arvind, plantation is not limited to tree planting drives. It is built 
as a community-led effort, where farmers, SHGs, schoolchildren, 
and panchayats come together to plant and care for trees over 
time. By integrating plantations into farmlands, school campuses, 
and shared commons, environmental stewardship becomes part of 
everyday life rather than a one-time activity.
Cultivating Stewardship
Wildlife Conservation: Enabling Coexistence Through 
Knowledge
As ecosystems expand and regenerate, the question is not only 
how to restore landscapes, but how to sustain the life they support. 
The recovery of the Asiatic lion is one of India’s most significant 
conservation successes, but it also presents a new reality. Today, 
over 50% of lions live outside protected areas, spread across a 35,000 
km² landscape where human activity and wildlife increasingly 
overlap, and less than 15% of this range is formally protected. 
In partnership with Ahmedabad University, Arvind supports long-
term research in the Greater Gir landscape to better understand 
how lions and other species navigate these shared spaces. This 
year marked the start of fieldwork, with a field station established 
in Amreli district and nearly 14,000 hours of sound data already 
collected. This enables large-scale mapping of wildlife presence 
and disturbances, building the foundation for monitoring systems 
that can be adopted by the Forest Department and scaled beyond

Dairy: Strengthening Everyday Incomes
In Gujarat dairy farming is a central pillar of rural livelihoods and 
largely managed by women. Livestock is often the most reliable 
source of household income: steady, daily, and within women’s 
control.
Arvind’s approach builds on this existing system with a simple but 
effective insight: for many families, adding just one more animal 
can significantly increase income within a short cycle. By facilitating 
access to local financing, and supporting farmers through animal 
health camps and training, the programme strengthens both 
productivity and earnings. 
Rural livelihood impactThe outcomes of education, livelihoods, and environmental 
resilience converge in one place: the quality of everyday life. The 
true measure of impact lies in how these changes are experienced 
at the household and community level.
Across the villages surrounding Arvind’s manufacturing locations, 
this means access to steady incomes, continuity in education, 
and opportunities that reduce the need for migration, building 
opportunity within the village itself.

1,600+850+ Digital Education: Expanding Access to Opportunity
In the villages surrounding Arvind’s manufacturing locations, the 
digital divide is less about access and more about opportunity, 
shaping the pathways available to young people. Bridging this gap 
early is critical to expanding future choices.
Arvind addresses this through two complementary models that 
work at different stages of the journey. For school students, HP 
CLAP vans, a mobile digital lab, a van equipped with 120 laptops 
and a trained instructor, brings structured, curriculum-linked 
learning directly to classrooms, building early familiarity and 
confidence. For youth, the HP World on Wheels (WOW) programme 
operates as a mobile classroom with 16  computer systems and an 
instructor, focused on digital upskilling and connecting learners to 
employment opportunities.
Together, these models ensure that digital access translates into 
real capability. Students move from unfamiliarity to confidence, 
becoming able to navigate the internet safely, use digital tools, and 
engage with a far wider universe of knowledge that opens pathways 
beyond the classroom.
300+ women dairy farmers have also come together to form a 
Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO), enabling them to move 
beyond individual livelihoods to collective enterprise. By 
aggregating production and improving market access, the FPO 
creates a pathway for women to take the next step from dairy 
farmers to entrepreneurs.
In FY27, we endeavour to take this programme to more women  
dairy farmers across our locations.

The Homestays: Creating Local Enterprise
In rural communities where livelihoods are limited and migration 
is common; Arvind’s homestay initiative in Narmada, creates an 
alternative rooted in the village itself. Families are supported to 
convert part of their homes into simple guest accommodations, 
leveraging existing spaces rather than requiring new infrastructure.
The model focuses on making this transition practical and 
viable. Households are supported with basic upgrades such 
as clean rooms, sanitation facilities, and bedding; trained in 
hospitality, hygiene, and guest management; and onboarded onto 
platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Homestays are also 
certified by Gujarat Tourism, ensuring quality standards and 
visibility. Local youth are engaged as coordinators, supporting day-
to-day operations and guest experience.
This enables families, particularly women to become 
microentrepreneurs from the comfort of their home and create a 
steady non-farm income stream while retaining control over how 
their culture and way of life is shared. 
We have created 37 homestays so far, with 4 created this year, 
supporting families with an alternative income that improves 
quality of life. 
NIOS: Creating Second Chances in Education
At the doors of our factories, we meet young people seeking work, 
many having left school after Class 8 or 10, and unable to meet 
minimum education criteria. What begins as a barrier to entry can 
become a long-term constraint on income and opportunity.
Arvind’s Open schooling programme responds directly to this 
reality. Through the Gujarat State Open Schooling (GSOS), learners 
are supported to complete their Class 10 and 12 education 
alongside work, with structured academic support and guidance. 
Whether it is a 14-year-old forced to leave school too soon, or a 
41-year-old who never had the chance to continue, the programme 
creates space for both.
By enabling education to resume, this year the programme opened 
pathways for 180 students towards employment, progression, and 
greater financial stability.92

Reviving & Promoting Art and 
Cultural Heritage
As a textile company, Arvind’s roots are closely tied to India’s 
cultural history, and more specifically to Ahmedabad’s rich legacy 
of textile, craft, and knowledge traditions. The story of indigo, the 
evolution of craft, and the knowledge systems that underpin them 
form part of a living legacy that continues to shape the present.
Preserving this heritage is not separate from our work, it is an 
extension of the same responsibility that guides our engagement 
with communities: to sustain what endures and preserve it for 
future generations. 
Indology: Preserving India’s Intellectual Heritage
India’s legacy does not live in monuments alone. It lives in its 
knowledge systems, in the manuscripts, texts, and scholarly 
traditions that have accumulated over centuries, carrying within 
them philosophy, science, medicine, literature, and law. Many of 
these materials are fragile, rare, and historically difficult to access. 
Without active intervention, they risk being lost entirely.
Indology is the academic study of Indian history, culture, and 
languages through ancient texts. Arvind’s Indology initiative 
supports the Lalbhai Dalpatbhai Museum of Indology, one of India’s 
most significant repositories of ancient manuscripts and scholarly 
materials, in its mission to preserve and activate this heritage 
through digitisation, conservation, and research.
By enabling access, scholarship, and interpretation, the 
initiative ensures that India’s intellectual heritage is not merely 
archived, but remains alive, relevant, and available to the 
scholars and communities who need it most.

Our Position: Arvind Limited is committed to addressing climate 
change and contributing to global sustainability goals through 
responsible business practices. As a signatory to the United Nations

and aligned with the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the 
United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
We do not engage in any lobbying activities, nor are the trade 
associations we are affiliated with involved in lobbying efforts. 
However, we conduct periodic reviews of all such affiliations to 
ensure continued alignment with our climate and sustainability 
priorities. Oversight is provided by the ESG Committee, with 
the Sustainability function’s highest executive or a designated 
representative responsible for evaluating such alignment and 
reporting to the Committee.
Beyond internal alignment, we actively contribute to collective 
sustainability progress by participating in industry associations

principles on which our governance policy is founded are:
• Satisfy the spirit and not just the letter of the law
• Corporate governance standards should go beyond the law
• Be transparent and maintain a high degree of disclosure.
• Make a clear distinction between personal conveniences and 
corporate resources
• Communicate externally, in a truthful manner, about how the 
Company is run internally
• Have a simple and transparent corporate structure driven solely 
by business needs
• The Management is the trustee, not the owner of

Board Accountability
At Arvind Limited, we uphold the highest standards of corporate 
governance, and board accountability forms a cornerstone of 
our governance framework. We ensure transparency, oversight, 
and effectiveness in board functioning through the following 
measures:
Board meeting attendance
The Company maintains a high level of participation and 
engagement with its directors. For FY26, the average board 
meeting attendance stood at 93%. Director-wise attendance is 
disclosed in the Corporate Governance Report.
Shareholder oversight on bylaws
Any material change in the Company’s bylaws requires 
the approval of shareholders. This ensures that significant 
governance decisions are subject to broader stakeholder scrutiny 
and consent.Board member mandates
Arvind Limited values the broad expertise and governance 
experience that its board members bring from various leadership 
roles. In line with our commitment to transparency and effective 
oversight, we also disclose the number of external directorships 
held by each board member. Individual details are available in 
the “Number of Directorships Held” table under Point 2 of the 
Corporate Governance Report.
Board performance evaluation
The Nomination and Remuneration Committee is responsible 
for evaluating the performance of the Board, its committees, 
and individual directors. This responsibility is formally included 
in the Committee’s Terms of Reference (ToR), ensuring that 
performance reviews are systematic, objective, and aligned 
with governance best practices.
Shared Ownership Requirements
There is no management ownership requirement for the CEO or 
other members of the executive committee at Arvind.

Arvind’s IT function is closely aligned with its core business 
objectives and plays a vital role in driving innovation, operational 
excellence, and value creation. By embedding technology 
across all business units, the Company has made IT central to its 
growth, enabling scalable digital ecosystems and continuous 
transformation.
Governance Oversight
The Board of Directors, through its Risk Management Committee, 
provides structured and systematic oversight of the Cybersecurity 
Governance Process. This ensures alignment with enterprise-wide 
risk frameworks and regulatory expectations. The Committee 
monitors cybersecurity risks, approves strategic initiatives related 
to IT and information security, and ensures that risk mitigation 
measures are implemented across the organisation.
Management Responsibility
At the management level, Mr. Nitin Parmar, Chief Information 
Officer (CIO), is responsible for the implementation and day-
to-day management of IT and cybersecurity across Arvind 
Limited. He oversees the execution of our IT strategy, ensures 
cybersecurity resilience, leads incident response and infrastructure 
improvements, and reports to the leadership team on emerging 
threats and mitigation measures.Key responsibilities and actions under IT management include:
• Business Continuity Plans: Information security-related 
continuity protocols maintained and tested at least annually to 
ensure preparedness.
• Vulnerability Analysis: Regular scanning and mitigation of 
system vulnerabilities, including annual third-party vulnerability 
Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT) to identify and 
address potential security gaps.
• Internal Audits: Periodic annual audits of IT infrastructure 
and information security systems to identify gaps and drive 
improvements.
• Incident Reporting & Escalation: A 24/7 dedicated IT helpline 
and helpdesk available for employees to report cybersecurity 
incidents or suspicious activity at any time.
• Awareness & Training: Continuous employee training 
programmes, with at least one annual session, to promote 
secure digital practices and maintain cyber hygiene.
Our Commitment
We are committed to protecting data, ensuring privacy, and 
maintaining the integrity of our systems. We continuously invest 
in advanced technologies and best practices to stay ahead of 
emerging cybersecurity threats. Additionally, we are conscious of 
our environmental footprint and strive to manage IT sustainably 
through energy-efficient infrastructure, renewable energy 
integration, and responsible e-waste disposal.

recommendation of the Audit Committee, has approved 
the appointment and remuneration of M/s. Kiran J. Mehta 
& Co., Cost Accountants, Ahmedabad as the Cost Auditors 
to conduct the audit of the cost records of the Company for 
the Financial Year ending March 31, 2027 at a remuneration 
of ₹4.15 Lakh (Rupees four lakh fifteen thousand only) plus 
applicable taxes and out-of-pocket expenses.
In accordance with the provisions of Section 148(3) of the 
Act read with The Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 
2014, the remuneration payable to the Cost Auditors has to 
be ratified by the members of the Company. Accordingly, 
consent of the Members is sought for passing an Ordinary 
Resolution as set out in Item No. 5 of the Notice for ratification 
of the remuneration payable to the Cost Auditors for the 
Financial Year ending March 31, 2027. 
None of the Directors or any Key Managerial Personnel or 
any relative of any of the Directors of the Company or the 
relatives of any Key Managerial Personnel is, in anyway, 
concerned or interested (financially or otherwise) in the 
above resolution.
The Board of Directors recommends the Ordinary Resolution 
set out in Item No. 5 for approval by the Members.
Item No. 6
The Non-Executive Directors (other than the Managing 
Director, Whole-time Directors) were paid commission not 
exceeding 1% per annum of the net profits of the Company in 
terms of the resolution passed by the Members at the Annual 
General Meeting held on August 18, 2021 and as decided by the Board of Directors of the Company. The said approval 
was valid for a period of five years from April 01, 2021 valid 
till March 31, 2026.
The said resolution has expired by efflux of time and accordingly 
in terms of Section 197, 198, Schedule V and other applicable 
provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, it is proposed to pass a 
fresh resolution by way of Special Resolution for the purpose 
of continuity of payment of such commission to Directors other 
than Managing Director and Whole-time Director for each 
Financial Year for further period of five (5) years commencing 
from April 01, 2026 to March 31, 2031.
To ensure alignment with the Company’s performance 
and good corporate governance, the actual commission 
payable to each Non-Executive Director within the overall 
1% limit shall be determined by the Board/Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee based on objective performance 
benchmarks. These criteria include the number of Board and 
Committee meetings attended, responsibilities undertaken 
(such as Chairmanship of critical committees like Audit and 
NRC) and the individual’s strategic guidance and contribution 
to the Company’s growth.
None of the Non-Executive Directors received any 
remuneration from Group Companies except Sitting Fees 
and Commission.
Further, the distribution of commission shall be structured 
such that no single Non-Executive Director receives more than 
50% of the total commission pool in any given Financial Year.
In the event of loss or inadequacy of profits in any Financial 
Year, the Company proposes to pay minimum remuneration 
as per Schedule V of the Act for a maximum period of three 
(3) years (from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2029). Other details 
pursuant to the provisions of Schedule V are as provided 
below:

Company’s Performance
FY26 commenced on a stable footing despite a challenging 
global macroeconomic environment. During the year, the 
Company proactively absorbed initial tariff pressures and 
strategically realigned its business mix, demonstrating 
resilience and operational discipline. These actions helped 
establish a strong foundation for the second half of the 
year, underscoring the Company’s ability to adapt swiftly to 
evolving market conditions. Consequently, the Company 
remained well positioned to respond effectively to ongoing 
disruptions while continuing to drive growth through market 
share gains and deeper customer engagement.
For the full year ended FY26, the Company recorded 
consolidated revenue of ₹9,303 Crores and EBITDA of  ₹1,061 Crores , translating into an EBITDA margin of 11.4%. 
Improved operating performance and disciplined working 
capital management supported robust free cash flow 
generation during the year. As a result, net debt reduced by 
₹112 Crores , closing at ₹1,172 Crores as at year end.
The Company’s Balance Sheet has been significantly 
strengthened over recent years through a disciplined 
capital allocation strategy, a streamlined debt profile, 
and an optimse capital structure. Consistent free cash 
flow generation has further enhanced financial flexibility, 
positioning the Company to pursue growth opportunities 
while maintaining Balance Sheet resilience.114
Arvind Limited | Integrated Annual Report 2025-2026
=== page 116 ===
These outcomes reflect the Company’s continued 
commitment to innovation, customer centricity, and 
sustainability, along with its proven ability to navigate a 
dynamic operating environment with agility and precision. 
Collectively, these efforts have further consolidated Arvind’s 
position as a trusted industry leader.
Strategic Developments
On May 06, 2026 the Company announced the acquisition 
of a ~61% controlling stake in U.S.-based Dalco GFT through 
its wholly owned Subsidiary, Arvind Advanced Materials 
Limited (AAML). This acquisition marks the Company’s entry 
into the world’s largest technical textiles market.
Dalco GFT , with a revenue base of ~US$100 million, EBITDA 
margins of ~17%, and ROCE of ~40%, strengthens AAML’s 
portfolio in specialise non woven materials and significantly 
enhances its global footprint. The transaction is margin and 
EPS accretive from the first year and is expected to unlock 
meaningful synergies through cross sourcing, customer 
expansion, and technology integration, thereby supporting 
the Company’s long term growth ambitions.
Sustainability and ESG Initiatives
During FY26, the Company made significant progress across 
its sustainability agenda:
• Commissioned hybrid captive power capacity in 
partnership with Torrent Power, achieving 60% captive 
energy sourcing, thereby reducing dependence on grid 
power and lowering Scope 2 emissions.
• Received Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) approval 
for its near-term, long term and net zero targets aligned 
to FY 2050 reinforcing the Company’s commitment to a 
credible, science aligned decarbonisation pathway.
• Operationalised India’s first supercritical CO₂ dyeing 
facility, a waterless dyeing technology that eliminates 
effluent discharge and significantly reduces energy 
consumption in wet processing.
• Entered into a strategic partnership with Circ Inc. (USA), 
a pioneer in hydrothermal textile recycling, to advance 
fibre to fibre circularity and enable closed loop solutions 
for blended fabrics.
• Launched India’s first industrial scale torrefaction 
project in collaboration with Peak Venture, converting 
agricultural biomass into a clean coal substitute and 
directly supporting fuel switching and Scope 1 emission 
reduction.
As a direct result of these tangible sustainability efforts, 
Arvind improved its S&P Global Corporate Sustainability 
Assessment (CSA) ESG Score to a record 74. This significantly 
exceeds the global industry average of 31 and earned the 
Company a global ranking of 6th worldwide (and 2nd in India) 
among peers in the textiles sector.Outlook
The evolving geopolitical situation in the Middle East has 
heightened uncertainty, impacting input costs, supply 
chains, and currency movements. While near term challenges 
persist, the Company remains well positioned to navigate 
this environment, supported by its diversified operations 
and strong product portfolio, which underpin margin 
resilience. Concurrently, the Company continues to focus on 
aligning stakeholder interests and enhancing returns over 
the medium to long term.
A more detailed analysis and commentary on the Company’s 
performance and outlook are provided in the Management 
Discussion and Analysis Section of this Integrated Annual 
Report.
